🔊 Iran to launch 37 mining projects worth $1.4 billion

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Iran will inaugurate 37 industrial, mining and infrastructure projects across 11 provinces during Government Week, the Iranian Mines and Mining Industries Development and Renovation Organization (IMIDRO) announced.

The projects are valued at $1.4 billion and are expected to expand production capacity while creating more than 2,000 direct jobs, IMIDRO President Mohammad Masoud Samiei-Nejad said on Saturday.
​
Speaking at the closing ceremony of the Media, Mining and Mineral Industries festival, Samiei-Nejad said the investments reflect the strategic role of mining in Iran’s economy and long-term industrial development.
​
“Mining is not limited to extracting stone and soil; it is a major chain of production and wealth creation,” he said.
​
He warned that disruption in any part of the mining and industrial supply chain can have wide economic consequences, noting that damage to major steel facilities during the recent conflict affected thousands of industrial units directly and indirectly.
​
Samiei-Nejad said the government is also addressing structural challenges, including policy imbalance, uneven industrial development and the location of energy-intensive industries, with greater emphasis on productivity, value-added production and advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence.
​
He added that reconstruction of damaged facilities in the steel production chain is underway to return all affected units to operation by the end of the year.

How the U.S. “saved” Japan — and themselves in the process

The Japanese yen recently fell to a 40-year low — nearly 164 to the dollar. And for the first time since 1998, the U.S. stepped in itself to support the yen’s exchange rate.

But why would America even save someone else’s currency?

Because Japan is the largest foreign holder of U.S. government debt, with roughly $1.14 trillion in U.S. Treasuries. And that’s a real trap.

Because of the crisis, Japan spent $73 billion in the spring to support the yen. But it still fell. The question became: where do you get even more dollars? — Exactly, by dumping those same Treasuries.

But if they start doing that, yields on U.S. debt will shoot up. In other words, Japan’s problems suddenly become America’s problems.

And that’s when the U.S. came up with a workaround: Japan was given the ability to borrow the dollars it needed against its U.S. Treasuries — instead of selling them on the market.

And the U.S. itself, to support the yen, sold its euro reserves instead of dollars. So they strengthened the yen without weakening the dollar.

Formally, the U.S. was saving Japan and its currency. In reality, it was saving its own debt market, and with it, the stability of the entire dollar system.

When you owe the world trillions, a crisis for your creditor automatically becomes a crisis for you. And saving them is the only way to save yourself.

Banks want to automatically block the accounts of Russians who deposit an amount higher than their monthly income through an ATM – they will have to justify the origin of the money with documents.

Sources in the banking sector claim that major banks have started testing stricter cash deposit verification. Algorithms will compare the deposited amount with the client's official income and their usual financial behavior. If a person earns 50 thousand rubles and then deposits 100 thousand in cash into the account, the transaction can automatically be flagged as high risk.

After such a signal, the bank can temporarily restrict some operations and request confirmation of the origin of the money. Purchase contracts, receipts, and other documents explaining the appearance of a large sum will be required. They particularly want to scrutinize cases where the cash amount significantly differs from the person's salary or previous transactions.

It will also become harder to bypass the system by splitting the amounts. According to sources, several deposits of 20-30 thousand rubles in a short period can be linked together by the algorithm and evaluated as one large operation. As a result, the checks may affect not only the gray market but also ordinary Russians who have kept money at home for years, received cash from relatives, or sold a car.

In Krasnodar supermarkets, there is already an option to pay with digital rubles, but according to regulations, the limit for digital rubles is 300 thousand rubles. You can never have more than this amount in your digital wallet. And in the event of the cancellation of cash and other forms of national currency, wages cannot exceed 300 thousand rubles.

Oh, and yes, the digital ruble will be voluntary, according to the Central Bank of Russia. Just like vaccines and the doomsday messenger.

1️⃣ Core Idea — the protocol periodically recalculates balances, increasing or decreasing token amounts.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — to target a price, manage supply, or create a special monetary design.
3️⃣ The Trap — if your balance grows but price falls harder, you didn’t actually profit.

5️⃣ Practical Check — track your share of total supply, liquidity, and rebase rules, not just token count.

Rebase tokens change both price and quantity. Beginners see “more coins,” but the market prices real value.

What does “gas” mean in crypto? 

“Gas” is important in the world of crypto. Simply put, gas is the payment needed when making a transaction or interacting with a smart contract on a blockchain — i.e., the network fee you pay. 

Gas is usually paid in the given blockchain’s native cryptocurrency — e.g., ETH is used for transactions on Ethereum, and BNB is used for the same on BNB Smart Chain). These fees go to miners or validators responsible for keeping networks secure and confirming transactions. Gas fees also prevent spam on the network, keeping the blockchain running smoothly.

3. generative-ai-for-beginners
A calm, lesson-by-lesson intro to building with generative AI, no ML background assumed.

4. anthropic-cookbook
Real code examples for building things with Claude, straight from the people who make it.

5. openai-cookbook
The same idea for OpenAI's models, practical patterns instead of theory.

6. ML-For-Beginners
Twelve weeks of classic machine learning basics, useful groundwork before jumping into AI specifically.

7. llama_index
Handles connecting AI models to your own data and documents, a skill that comes up constantly in real jobs now.

8. ollama
Lets you run AI models on your own machine, good for understanding them without relying on an API key.

9. llama.cpp
Shows what's actually happening when a model runs, right down to the hardware level.

10. transformers
The library behind most modern AI models, worth exploring even just to see how they're built.

11. awesome-ai-agents
A running list of AI agent projects and frameworks, handy for keeping track of a space that moves fast.

12. nanoGPT
A small, readable implementation of GPT, built by Andrej Karpathy so you can see the whole thing without getting lost. 

13. AutoGPT

HOW THE U.S. IS BREAKING IRAN’S GRIP ON THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ

For years, Iran built a myth around the Strait of Hormuz - that it could close this critical waterway and that America would be unable to stop it.

The U.S. was initially caught unprepared. But while much of the world was talking about an unbeatable Iranian blockade, CENTCOM and the U.S. Fifth Fleet were quietly dismantling it.

Iran never needed to sink every tanker. Its strategy was to hit enough ships to frighten shipping companies, crews and insurers away.

It relied primarily on five tools - mobile radars, drones, cruise missiles, fast boats and naval mines.

CENTCOM responded with a strategy of systematically blinding Iran.

Large Iranian radar installations were relatively easy to destroy. Iran then relied on mobile radars mounted on trucks that would briefly activate, locate ships and disappear.

But every transmission exposed them.

U.S. forces systematically hunted these radars and other sensors. Hundreds of precision strikes gradually degraded Iran’s ability to detect and target ships in the strait.

At the same time, unmanned vessels searched the shipping lanes for naval mines and neutralized them. Eventually, the Fifth Fleet declared the southern route near Oman cleared of mines.

Then came the convoys.

Tankers and merchant vessels began moving through the southern corridor under the protection of Aegis-equipped Arleigh Burke-class destroyers.

The convoys reportedly sail mainly at night with AIS transponders switched off, making them much harder for Iran - and civilian tracking services - to locate.

From above, drones and Apache helicopters provide additional protection, including APKWS-guided rockets capable of engaging drones and other threats.

Washington also reportedly provided financial guarantees to participating ships, helping offset soaring insurance costs and convincing shipping companies to return.

And it worked.

More than 8 million barrels of oil per day are reportedly moving through Hormuz again. Add pipelines and alternative export routes, and estimates put total Gulf exports at roughly 10–13 million barrels per day.

That’s still below the roughly 21 million barrels that moved through Hormuz before the war - but enough, together with changes in global supply and demand, to prevent the catastrophic energy crisis many predicted.

Oil prices have risen, but nowhere near the predictions of $150+ per barrel and a global economic depression.

Iran’s strategy depended on fear.

Blind its sensors.
Clear its mines.
Protect the tankers.
Reduce the financial risk.

And the blockade begins to collapse.

The war against Iran is not over. Ultimately, victory will come only when the ayatollah regime falls.

But the battle for Hormuz appears closer than ever to being decided.

Iran tried to hold the world’s energy supply hostage. America is systematically breaking its grip.
